notes.title: A little bit about the factions...
notes.notes:
Some players might not yet be aware that there are a multitude of ways to build decks in DungeonTop. This is due to the lovely and somewhat complex cross intersection of your hero class (which determines your spells and skills) and your faction (which determines your minions).

The green faction have strong units capable of evolving into fearsome beasts that can match the enemies in the dungeon itself.

The red faction have fast agile and aggressive units which aren't necessarily the greatest defenders, but they sure do pack a punch!

The black faction is as you guessed the most nuanced, having a delicate balance between self inflicted wounds and power.

So that's a brief rundown. Be sure to check out the demo incase you haven't already!

Till next time.

Enjoy!

PS. In the meantime let me know if you plan on getting a steam deck. Those things look pretty awesome!

notes.title: Class distinction
notes.notes:
Little is known about our protagonists beginnings, yet their play styles are very distinct!

Here's a simply breakdown of the three classes currently available.

The warrior is a powerful basic class that gets strong healing and survivability talents. Recommended for first-time players.

The mage is an initially difficult class that relies more on spells than on minions. It is offered less minions in drops and has less health than the other classes.

The rogue is a medium difficulty class that balances spells and minions. It has moderate health compared to the other classes.

Stay tuned and soon we'll go over the various factions and which widen you opportunity to construct the ultimate deck!

notes.notes:
Merry Christmas!

In Seasons Mode, at the end of a battle there is a chance to pick a Present or a Stolen card.

Presents contain a random lower level card marked as Nice.
Stolen Cards are higher level cards but they are marked as Naughty.
Nice and Naughty cards perform a random effect when they are played.
Enemies also play Naughty and Nice Cards.

notes.title: Beginner Mode
notes.notes:
Tailoring balance to a wide range of players has always been a challenge, but one we've strived to achieve.

Listening to the feedback of those less experienced with card games or roguelike deckbuilders has brought us valuable insight regarding the onboarding experience.

So we're excited to bring new players a fresh beginning and easier transition into the genre!

When selecting new game, player chooses between beginner and normal mode.

An Easier Experience of DungeonTop, Recommended for those inexperienced with card games.
- Heal after each battle
- More Card choices and selections after battles
- Less gold earned than Normal Mode

notes.title: Reaper Mode
notes.notes:
Halloween Update: Reaper Mode 

Happy Halloween, Dungeontop Players! We've got a new content update for you today, and in the spirit of spooky season, it's Halloween-themed. 

In the world above the Dungeon, it's Hallowtide, where the walls between the realms of the living and dead grow thin, and it's time to put out your candies to keep the dead away from the doors. But the Reaper does not stalk above this year - He's trapped in the Dungeon too, and willing to do business.

Activating Reaper Mode from the main menu will enable Permadeath for your faction minions - Meaning that any minion that dies in combat will be removed from your deck. No more suicide blocking for your hero, because every minion life is precious! 

But if you lose that precious 3-Star Wyrm, you can get it back, for a price; Pumpkin Jack, the Reaper Man, can be found as a shop in the dungeon, trading in souls. 

Reaper Mode has the same Ferocity grading as the regular dungeon, but the factions are locked - Start with Green, then Red, then Black. Black, especially, is incredibly difficult to win with in this mode. I want to see screenshots if anyone manages an F15 Black run!

notes.title: Roguelike deckbuilding meets board-based battles in Spellsword Cards: DungeonTop
notes.notes:
Long ago, Duelyst pioneered the magical game combination of deck and board. You’d build up an arsenal of tricksy monsters, then move them around while thinking about abilities and adjacency bonuses and the safety of your ‘you’ character. That was against online opponents, but Spellsword Cards: DungeonTop takes the same idea and runs with it through Slay The Spire-like dungeons. The roguelike deckbuilder came out on early access last week, and I have found it moreish.

notes.title: Early Access Ready
notes.notes:
Thank you, Everyone! 

Our Early Access launch is coming soon and above all we just wanted to thank all the alpha testers who have helped shape the game from its simple beginnings into what it is now. Without your help the project would be very different, and probably a lot worse. 

We’ve been a little quiet over the Christmas and new years break, what with the holiday season + the devastating bushfires here in Australia. However, we’ve still been hard at work getting the game ready, and I’m happy to say that today we have decided to lock the game content ahead of our Jan 15th launch. We’re EA-Ready! 

What Does This Mean? 
There will be no major content pushes this coming week as we focus entirely on ironing out any annoying bugs that crop up. We can still make balance changes, however, so if something’s not working quite right, let us know.

notes.title: Better Treasures, Encounter Complexity
notes.notes:
[b]Better Treasures[/b]

One of the core pillars of Dungeontop’s design is strategic choices. We’ve been trying to push this angle with every content push going forward, and one of the areas we could see this failing was the treasure cards.

Previously, the treasure cards all gave reasonably powerful effects, but were consumed on use. The thinking here was to provide a choice between using these cards and cashing them in at the shops, but this was flawed thinking; With this design, the cards were only considered usable when your back was really against the wall, and even then, they didn’t feel good to use. All they’d end up doing was bricking in your hand when you were stable, getting you into a bad situation later down the line and force you to use them anyway.
The new treasures do not consume on use. They are also powerful, at par or sometimes even better than level 1-2 cards from drops. We hope that this encourages you to think long-term about their use - Maybe you want to keep them now and upgrade later? Or maybe it’s better to reduce deck pollution early even if it drops your overall power level right now?
Only time and testing will prove if this change is truly better, but from early feedback in the Discord, it seems to be a well-received change.

[b]Encounter Complexity[/b]

Those of you who have been playing since the beginning of alpha stage may notice a significant decrease in the difficulty of encounters on the first floor.
This is for two reasons, the first being onboarding - If you’ve been playing for a little while and are already comfortable with our mechanics, you may not have noticed, but the game had quite a sharp learning curve. We’re trying to tamp that down as much as possible to make the first-time experience more enjoyable.
The second is reduction in complexity, which does not necessarily equate to making the game easier. During this alpha stage, we’ve made a lot of very complicated mechanics. Some of these have been very fun to engage with, some decidedly were not (Looking at you, Cleave + Guardian). As we remove some of these junk mechanics, we’re also trying to boil down the best mechanics to keywords to prevent the ‘word salad’ problem some of our cards have and reduce the amount of reading you need to do. Ideally, you should be able to understand most encounters within one pass of reading, and even our most complex encounters should not take more than a second scan to parse. If this isn’t the case, we have a problem, and we’d like to hear about it.

Thanks,

Bryn ‘Jammy’ Welch
DungeonTop Designer
